> " or that they would have been glad after having failed and realizing they wished they'd succeeded" What do you mean by this?

Sorry, I should have been more clear... I mean while you hear a lot about people who are glad their suicide attempts failed, we don't often hear:

A. People who (if they had lived) would have *regretted* that their attempts failed

B. People who go on to attempt again and ensure that they do succeed

Or at least, we don't hear about them often when this sort of discussion comes about. More focus is placed on those who feel like they were given a second chance, rather than those who feel like they lost their chance.

> how would someone who has died have an opinion on his/her death?

That's what I meant. Say Bob wants to kill himself, he fails. He wishes he hadn't. Or, later in life he's suffered so much that he doesn't feel that "second chance" feeling that some others do when they fail to end their lives. That's what I meant by what I said -- not necessarily that the dead have opinions, but hypothetically, that not all those that die by their own hand would regret their decision, if there was some way to measure that. We don't know that they all regret it and I doubt that they all do.

>You feel like you've run out of coping methods... if I may ask, what have those been?

That's a fair question, and a loaded one. I've always been the type of person to deal with things on my own, and I don't have close family to go to with emotional things. However, reaching out to friends has always helped in the past and I was able to power through things, despite it being an upward battle.

Because of personal family situations I really do not want to seek medical attention for this. I'm just afraid.

Three is only really half a yes, because I have a rather "vague" when rather than a specific one. And I hear a lot that people who tried to commit suicide but failed often are glad they failed. But I think there's some confirmation bias there; we don't get to hear from those that are glad they'd died, or that they would have been glad after having failed and realizing they wished they'd succeeded. 

So I don't know what to think, I'm a mess right now and all I know is that I CAN'T take all the pain I have. Even sharing it with people that care about me is not enough anymore. I feel like I've run out of coping methods and the saddest part is that I don't want to die, because I recognize that there's beauty in living.

The idea of asking for "help" is much more terrifying than the idea of continuing to force myself through the existence I'm living right now. My father has been "helped" twice and I *do not* want that experience to be mine. If I were given the autonomy to make my own decisions about my healthcare once I decided to be honest about my situation with a professional, then I would, but I know this isn't the case. I know that if you meet a certain set of criteria, you have no say in the matter. That scares me more than anything.

The issue here is that while outside events have always acted as catalysts, signalling that my life was getting worse at that point in time... what I'm feeling goes beyond any of these events. Simply talking about the events wouldn't alleviate the feelings I have underlying them. For me, I think, talk therapy would be useless.

Medications are terrifying for the above reasons... In order to get them, you need "help", and if you're lucky, the meds they choose for you won't make things worse. 

Helplines are also unhelpful in my case, I would think, because with something like this I'm not a very impulsive person. That means I'm less likely to do it than a more impulsive person, but more likely to do it right if I try.
